title: Keeping the Path amid Change: Ritual Transmission and Religious Transformation Among Tahtacı Alevis in Western Anatolia
content: This article asks how religious transformation affects the capacity of Tahtacı Alevi communities in Western Anatolia to reproduce ritual knowledge across generations. Drawing on multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2021 and 2026 in thirteen settlements in İzmir, Aydın, Muğla, and Denizli, including participant observation and interviews with twenty-five participants, it compares five ritual and moral domains: the three-knotted belt, Hak Üleştirme, Yas Nefesi and funerary practice, Öznek, and Hearth Digging. Rather than treating transformation as either rupture or preservation, the article develops “Keeping the Path” as an ethnographically grounded framework of religious transmission. It identifies five interacting mechanisms: boundary work and communal recognition, relational authority, intergenerational participation, embodied and oral-musical learning, and selective adaptation. The findings reveal uneven reproductive capacity. Practices embedded in multiple settings of family life, communal obligation, ritual authority, and everyday moral evaluation remain comparatively resilient, whereas practices dependent on infrequent occasions or narrowly distributed musical and procedural competence are more vulnerable. By distinguishing cultural recognition from performative competence, the study argues that transformation is best understood as a reorganization of transmission ecologies. The Tahtacı case contributes to contemporary Alevi Studies and broader debates on lived religion, authority, memory, and religious change.
